core: Definition of social role as expected behavior attached to a social position
Status vs role distinction (position vs expected behavior)
Role sets (one position, many roles; Merton 1957)
Role conflict vs role strain distinction
Role performance and Goffman's dramaturgical framing
Honest limits: roles shape but do not imprison
supporting: Linton (1936) as the classic formulation of status and role
outOfScope: Parsons' sick role and full role-theory frameworks

claims.claim: A social role is the expected behavior attached to a social position; sociologists describe roles as patterns of behavior that are representative of a person's social status.
Status and role are distinct: status is the rank a person holds in a social hierarchy, with attendant rights and duties, while role is the behavior expected of someone holding that status.

Ascribed status is assigned at birth or by circumstances beyond a person's control (e.g., age, family relationships), while achieved status is gained through choice and individual effort (e.g., an occupation).
A single status carries a role set, an array of roles attached to it; the concept is attributed to Robert K. Merton (1957).
Role strain arises when too much is required of a single role; the term is classically associated with William J. Goode's 1960 article 'A Theory of Role Strain' in the American Sociological Review.
Role conflict arises when the demands of two or more roles are contradictory or incompatible.

Role performance is how a person expresses a role; Erving Goffman (1959) compared social life to a stage and described impression management, in which people present themselves as actors performing for an audience.
The word 'role' was borrowed from theatrical usage, and it emphasizes the distinction between the actor and the part.

Roles shape behavior but do not erase individuality: a role remains relatively stable across different occupants, yet each person performs it with a unique style within the boundaries of expected behavior.
The classic formulation of status and role goes back to Ralph Linton's 1936 book The Study of Man, which treated roles as the behavioral prescriptions attached to statuses.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Role theory as a grand framework vs role as a working concept
positions: Mid-twentieth-century role theory treated roles as a comprehensive account of social life.

The Oxford Dictionary of Sociology (via Encyclopedia.com) notes that role theory came under sustained criticism, was seen as flawed, and fell out of use as a grand framework — while the concept of role remains a basic tool of sociological understanding.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the concept descriptively — role, status, role set, role conflict, role strain, role performance — as a working vocabulary, and includes the honest note that roles shape but do not imprison.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is a role the expected behavior or the actual behavior?
positions: A few writers equate 'role' with a person's actual behavior.
Most sociologists distinguish role as expected behavior from role behavior as its enactment (International Encyclopedia of the Social Sciences).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson follows the mainstream distinction used by OpenStax and Britannica: role is the expected behavior attached to a position; how a person expresses it is role performance.

sourceRecords.title: Role
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. britannica.com blocks direct fetch (HTTP 403); read 2026-08-22 via Wayback Machine capture 20160105011152 of the canonical URL. Supports: role as the behavior expected of an individual who occupies a given social position or status; the term borrowed from theatrical usage, emphasizing the distinction between the actor and the part; a role remains relatively stable even though different people occupy the position; an individual may have a unique style exhibited within the boundaries of expected behavior; individuals usually occupy several positions at once. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Social status
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. britannica.com blocks direct fetch; read 2026-08-22 via Wayback Machine capture 20151127110620 of the canonical URL. Supports: social status as the relative rank an individual holds, with attendant rights, duties, and lifestyle, in a social hierarchy; status may be ascribed (assigned at birth without reference to innate abilities) or achieved (requiring special qualities, gained through competition and individual effort); ascribed status typically based on sex, age, race, family relationships, or birth; achieved status based on education, occupation, accomplishments, or other factors. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
